bottleneck: Epigenetic and proteomic 'brain age' clocks predict cognitive decline and mortality, but what they measure — and whether the clock can be turned back — is unclear. A clock that correlates with aging without capturing its mechanism cannot guide intervention: different clocks disagree on individuals, and no one knows which clock's ticking corresponds to which causal process. Brain aging lacks both a definition and a validated reversibility test, so rejuvenation trials cannot tell whether they worked. The measurement problem precedes the treatment problem.
current_state: Clocks predict mortality and dementia risk robustly, but no intervention has been shown to reverse brain age on any validated measure, and mechanistic interpretation is missing.

sources.title: Brain Connectome: Mapping Neural Networks in Neuroscience

title: Brain aging clocks measure unknown mechanisms
why_it_blocks: You cannot treat aging without measuring it, and you cannot trust a measurement you do not understand. Mechanistic clocks would make brain rejuvenation testable — and unfalsifiable hype distinguishable from real progress.
